passage:
Dear Elizabeth,
I went to the group on Thursday, the one I told you about. I sat by the door with my coat on for twenty minutes. Then a man in a green cap said, "Nobody here will judge you, we've all said worse." I cried a little and nobody rushed to fix me. Someone just passed tissues. I said out loud that I'd been drinking every night since March, and the room stayed warm. I walked home lighter than I've felt in months. I'm going back next week and I'll keep telling the truth there. But a part of me worries I could start needing their clapping more than my own steadiness, so I'll keep calling you too. Maybe one day I'll be the one passing tissues.
Love,
Salma

qa.a: Going back next week, telling the truth there, staying in touch with Elizabeth, and maybe one day helping others as someone passing tissues.

qa.a: He probably recognised the nervousness from his own start, since he said everyone there has said worse, and wanted Salma to feel safe.

passage:
Facilitator's note, Tuesday evening group, community hall.

Gargi came for the third time tonight. The first week she stood by the door with her dupatta twisted around her fingers and left before tea. The second week she stayed but didn't speak.

Tonight, when we went around the circle, she said, "I'm Gargi. I've been betting on cricket apps for a year." Her voice was barely audible. Nobody gasped. Mohit, who has been coming for two years, said, "Welcome. Same here." Her shoulders dropped visibly.

After the meeting she asked if she could come early next week to help set up chairs. I said yes. I also mentioned the one-to-one counsellor at the district hospital, since the group works best alongside other support, and she took the leaflet.

Will check in with her next Tuesday. - Gurpreet

qa.q: How many times had Gargi come to the group by that evening?
qa.a: Gargi had come for the third time.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel when Mohit said "Welcome. Same here", and how can you tell?
qa.a: Gargi felt relieved and accepted; her shoulders dropped visibly after she spoke.

qa.q: Why was Gurpreet right to mention the one-to-one counsellor?
qa.a: The group helps most alongside other support, so Gargi does not rely only on the group for her recovery.

qa.q: How might Mohit see Gargi's first words in the circle?
qa.a: Mohit probably remembers what a first time in the circle feels like and wants Gargi to feel welcome.

grounding: The facilitator's note shows a young woman welcomed without judgement by a support group, feeling relief and belonging while being pointed to wider help.

passage:
Thursday night.

Fourth meeting. I spoke for the first time about the 3 am scrolling and the lectures I've missed since August. I thought they'd look at me like my family does, like I'm lazy. Instead a man called Anand, maybe thirty, nodded and said, "I lost a job to that exact thing." Someone passed me the biscuits. That's all. I felt so relieved I nearly cried in the car park.

I'm Sonali, and I haven't felt part of anything in a long time.

But I noticed something on the way home. I kept replaying whether they liked what I said. Whether I was a good member. That's the same itch as the phone, wanting the next little reward.

So: I'll keep going on Thursdays. I'll be honest. And I'll also see the college counsellor on Monday so this group isn't the only thing holding me up.

qa.q: How old did Anand seem to Sonali?
How did Sonali feel after speaking at the meeting, and what shows it?
qa.a: Sonali felt relieved and accepted, nearly crying in the car park and feeling part of something.

qa.a: Sonali will keep attending and stay honest, but also see the college counsellor so the group's approval is not the only support.

qa.q: How might Anand see Sonali's first time speaking?
qa.a: Anand likely recognises his own past in that story, and the nod says the struggle is shared.

grounding: The diary shows a young person accepted without judgement by a support group, feeling relief while watching out for depending only on the group's approval.
